extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and writers interested in the craft and criticism of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for evaluating and writing the 'story' aspect of the novel (how narrative of events in time functions, its effects, devices, and pros/cons). Draws on examples (Scott, Scheherazade, Bennett, Tolstoy) to illustrate what makes a story effective or defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel’s sensitiveness (not subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The novel’s success lies in its own sensitiveness, not in the success of its subject matter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novel develops when it acquires new sensitiveness (a 'fresh coat of quicksilver'). Changes in history or social movements do not automatically improve the novel; what matters is the writer's internal sensibility. Examples: novels written about revolutions often end up dominated by the writer’s memories and passions rather than the historical subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final test: reader’s affection
rubrics_metrics.description: “The final test of a novel will be our affection for it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal affection (the human heart) is the ultimate re-examiner of principles and systems in novel criticism. Critical judgments must allowance for this subjective test, though it can be distorted by sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control sentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: “Sentimentality shall not speak too loudly or too soon.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentimentality is an intrusive bias that can prematurely influence judgement ('Oh, but I like that'). Critics and writers should be aware of sentimental reactions and not let them dominate evaluation; the intensely human quality of a novel is unavoidable, but excessive sentimentality weakens critical clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven aspects to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects selected for discussion are seven in number: The Story; People; The Plot; Fantasy; Prophecy; Pattern; Rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the dimensions the lecturer proposes as useful ways of looking at a novel and the novelist’s work. Each aspect is a distinct lens for evaluation and craft decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Story (time-sequenced narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The story … is a narrative of events arranged in their time sequence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a story, its single merit is making the audience want to know what happens next; its single fault is making the audience not want to know what happens next. The story is the backbone of a novel — primitive and ancient — and must be judged primarily on its ability to sustain curiosity/suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense as core mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Story’s primary device is suspense: keeping the reader wondering 'what will happen next?' (illustrated by Scheherazade).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspense is the 'only literary tool that has any effect' on primitive curiosity; it can be used even when other qualities (description, character) are incidental. Effective storytelling often hinges on the skillful generation and maintenance of suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of temporal structure in a novel
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is never possible for a novelist to deny time inside the fabric of his novel: he must cling … to the thread of his story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novelist cannot completely abolish temporal progression inside the narrative; time-sense (a 'clock') is the basis of story. Experimental devices (turning the clock upside down, altering the hands) are legitimate, but they do not negate the temporal basis — they must still ensure intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish story from plot
rubrics_metrics.description: “A story, by the way, is not the same as a plot. … the plot is an organism of a higher type.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate chronological narration (story) with plot, which is a higher-order structuring of events and meaning. Evaluation and craft should treat plot-building and story-telling as different skills and purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice and oral quality of the story
rubrics_metrics.description: “The story is the aspect … which asks to be read out loud … it appeals not to the eye … but to the ear.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story-telling carries a voice that benefits from oral reading; the opening sentence of a story may lack visual beauty but loses something if not heard. The story transforms readers into listeners; voice is central to its effect even if it does not supply the author's full personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story-teller’s permissive technique (ragged ends, incidental episodes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story-teller can profit by 'ragged ends' and may introduce incidents or characters that lead nowhere; the storyteller 'keeps just as well within the simple boundaries of his art if he says things that have no bearing on the development.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodic, loose, or seemingly irrelevant material can be a legitimate storytelling choice (example: Scott's introductions and ragged ends). Storytelling values continuity of curiosity over strict cause-and-effect construction; critics should not demand causal tightness from every story-teller style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story’s primitiveness and its cultural effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “The story is primitive … it appeals to what is primitive in us. That is why we are so unreasonable over the stories we like … Intolerance is the atmosphere stories generate.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because stories tap deep, primitive tastes (suspense, curiosity), they can provoke strong, unreasonable preferences and intolerance of other forms. Critics and writers should recognize the emotional, non-rational pull of story-liking when evaluating literary merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novels should incorporate 'life by values' as well as 'life in time'
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily life is composed of two lives — the life in time and the life by values; a good novel includes the life by values as well as narrating the life in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond chronological events, novels should use devices (to be examined in other aspects) to convey intensity, values, and the qualitative life that does not map onto minutes and hours. Failure to incorporate value-life leaves a novel merely a sequence of events and can result in shallowness (examples: contrast between mere time-celebration and works that summon space or values like Tolstoy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique and tradition change across generations
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been a technique in English fiction which does alter from generation to generation (e.g., technique of laughing at characters, fantasy execution, use of 'he said'/'she said').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should examine literary tradition and technique because execution (the 'how') changes and influences perception; examples: differences in humor, fantasy, and dialogue-tag usage between centuries. However, lack of chronological study can limit the critic's appreciation of these shifts.
